summary: This chunk adds two new files. `docs/plans/brief-artifact-plan.md` is a plan for a new `brief-artifact` skill that reads large prose/code/diff artifacts and produces a layered brief (TL;DR, structure map, per-chunk summaries, claims with anchors/status, ranked risks, least-confident block), matching the layout of `skills/rule-audit/`. It specifies a chunker script, a chunk JSON schema, a renderer, and a SKILL.md workflow, plus eval fixtures. `resources/efficient-debug-loop-strategies.md` is an unrelated research report/playbook on debugging with Claude Code: verification-driven debugging, context management (`/compact`, `/clear`), prompting strategies, hooks, and common LLM-agent anti-patterns.

claims.text: The plan creates `skills/brief-artifact`, a skill reading prose/code/diff artifacts and writing a layered brief
Input types are prose docs, code files/dirs, and git diffs; output is `<artifact>.brief.md` plus terminal printout
Reading strategy: under 4 chunks read sequentially in main context, 4+ chunks fan out to one subagent per chunk
Claim status values are limited to verified, unverified, or contradicted (two anchors in same artifact disagree); no external lookups
risk_tier is 'high' when a code chunk touches auth, DB, IO, or dependency files (via regex list), else 'low'; prose is always 'low'
render_brief.py rejects invalid chunk JSON with the chunk id and exit code 1, because the agent must re-run that chunk rather than ship a hole
Verification-driven debugging (test-first) is described as Anthropic's most strongly endorsed pattern for Claude Code
Chroma's 'Context Rot' report (July 14, 2025) evaluated 18 frontier models and found performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows
Anthropic's Claude Code docs recommend running `/clear` after being corrected more than twice on the same issue in one session
Spracklen et al.'s USENIX Security 2025 study found 19.7% of recommended packages across 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs were hallucinated (205,474 unique fake names)

Extended-thinking token budgets (~4,000 for 'think', ~10,000 for 'think hard'/'megathink', 31,999 for 'ultrathink') come from Simon Willison's reverse-engineering, not Anthropic's official text, and his decompilation found 'think harder' and 'ultrathink' both map to 31,999, contradicting the blog's implied strict ordering

risks.note: 19.7% hallucination rate and 205,474 fake package count are attributed to a named study but no link/DOI is given in this chunk, so the figure can't be checked from the chunk alone.

Specific token counts (4,000 / 10,000 / 31,999) for extended-thinking levels are sourced to an external reverse-engineering blog post, not a primary/official source, and are flagged by the doc itself as approximate and version-dependent.

'Anthropic's own multi-agent research system consumed roughly 15× more tokens than a plain chat' is stated as fact but the chunk itself later caveats it as context-specific and not from Claude Code debugging.
